passage_records.claim: True-label logprob gradients and normalized kernel

passages.text: We propose to use a kernel comparing the input gradients of the particles,

where \kappa is a base kernel between gradients \nabla_{\mathbf{x}}f(\mathbf{x};\theta)_{y} that are of same size as the inputs \mathbf{x} . In essence, we define k as the expected similarity between the input gradients of two networks with respect to the data distribution p(\mathbf{x},y) . Interestingly, by using the kernel k , the KDE approximation \hat{\rho} of the particle distribution not only depends on the particles themselves but also depends on the data distribution. We approximate the kernel k using the training samples, with linear complexity:

The kernel only compares the gradients of the true label \nabla_{\mathbf{x}}f(\mathbf{x}_{n};\theta)_{y_{n}} , as opposed to the entire Jacobian matrix \nabla_{\mathbf{x}}f(\mathbf{x}_{n};\theta) , as our motivation is to encourage each particle to learn different features that could explain the training sample (\mathbf{x}_{n},y_{n}) well. This approach also reduces computational complexity, since automatic differentiation libraries such as JAX ( Bradbury et al., 2018 ) or Pytorch ( Paszke et al., 2019 ) would require \mathcal{C} passes, one per class, to calculate the full Jacobian.
We choose the RBF kernel on the unit sphere as our base kernel \kappa :

where \mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}^{\prime} denote the two normalized gradients of two particles with respect to one input, and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D} is a diagonal matrix containing squared lengthscales. We design \kappa to be norm-agnostic since the norm of the true label gradient ||\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}f(\mathbf{x}_{n};\theta)_{y_{n}}||_{2} fluctuates during training and as training converges, the log-probability f(\mathbf{x}_{n};\theta)_{y_{n}}=\log p(y_{n}|\mathbf{x}_{n},\theta) will approach \log 1 , leading to the norm ||\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}f(\mathbf{x}_{n};\theta)_{y_{n}}||_{2} approaching 0 due to the saturation of the log-softmax activation. Furthermore, comparing the normed input gradients between ensemble members teaches them to learn complementary explanatory patterns from the training samples, which could improve robustness of the ensemble. The RBF kernel is an apt kernel to compare unit vectors ( Jayasumana et al., 2014 ) , and we can control the variances of the gradients along input dimensions via the square lengthscales \boldsymbol{\Sigma} .

passage_records.claim: Biased minibatch repulsion and extra differentiation

passages.text: To make FoRDE amenable to mini-batch gradient optimization, we adapt the kernel in Eq. 10 to a mini-batch of samples \mathcal{B}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{b},y_{b})\}_{b=1}^{B} :

In principle, this kernel in the update rule in Eq. 8 leads to biased stochastic gradients of the repulsion term because the average over batch samples in Eq. 16 is inside the logarithm. However, in practice, we found no convergence issues in our experiments.

Compared to DEs, FoRDEs take roughly three times longer to train. In addition to a forward-backward pass to calculate the log-likelihood, we need an additional forward-backward pass to calculate the input gradients, and another backward pass to calculate the gradients of the input gradient repulsion with respect to the weights. This analysis is confirmed in practice: in resnet18 / cifar-100 experiments of Section 5.2 with an ensemble size of 10, a DE took \sim 31 seconds per epoch on an Nvidia A100 GPU, while FoRDE took \sim 101 seconds per epoch.

conclusion.verified_title: Bayesian Graph Convolutional Neural Networks using Node Copying
conclusion.saved_takeaway: Feature/label-conditioned correlated neighborhood replacement and conditional weight inference
verified_method_scope_summary: A base classifier supplies predicted-label groups; each node samples a donor from its predicted group.
Node copying changes the neighborhood to the donor's observed neighborhood while keeping node features unchanged.
Graph inference depends on observed topology, features and training labels.
The prose and Algorithm 1 train a GCNN over each sampled graph and use MC dropout for its conditional weights.
The printed v1 prediction factors in Eqs. (6)–(7) use G_obs; this differs from BGCN's prediction on sampled G and is preserved as a scope caveat.
qualification_limits: Node classification and neighborhood copying, not private NCNC completion scorers.
Do not silently replace G_obs with sampled G in the printed predictive equations.
Conditional fitting is approximate, not proof of exact Bayesian calibration.
conclusion.adoption: Use as prior for task-conditioned graph uncertainty and correlated neighborhood alternatives; qualify the printed inference graph.

conclusion.saved_takeaway: Learned stochastic connection masks, effective edge-weight interpretation and factorized variational training
verified_method_scope_summary: A mask has the same sparsity as the input adjacency, and the graph operator uses A times Z elementwise.
The paper interprets masked messages as edge-associated effective weight matrices.
§3.2 factorizes q(W,Z)=q(W)q(Z) and uses q(W)=delta(W-M), so this inspected construction does not preserve arbitrary posterior dependence between global model weights and masks.
§4 learns hierarchical beta-Bernoulli sampling rates alongside GNN parameters, with Kumaraswamy variational rates and either relaxed gradients or ARM.
qualification_limits: Observed-edge masking cannot add a missing edge where input A is zero.
The variational family is factorized and the global model-weight distribution is a point mass in the inspected formulation.
§5 local random-walk masking and complete predictive-uncertainty implementation were not freshly read; prior packet is separately cited.
conclusion.adoption: Do not present learned mask/model training or edge-associated stochastic weights as new; do not equate these masks with NCNC missing-edge completion.

conclusion.saved_takeaway: Missing-edge inflation, learned target-link-specific stochastic reduction, shared encoder and nonlinear link prediction
verified_method_scope_summary: Complete scores candidate nonedges with at least one common neighbor, adds top-k edges, and keeps inflated edges out of training labels.
Reduce conditions edge sampling probabilities on edge representation and target-link subgraph pooling; Bernoulli/Gumbel sampling trains a nonlinear subgraph predictor.
Predictor and reducer can share the same GNN encoder; completion-origin features and score buckets inform added-edge use.
Appendix B.3 explicitly uses expected edge probabilities as inference weights, rather than sampled graph prediction averaging.
Theorem 1 assumes a deterministic invertible local-neighborhood-to-link-probability mapping and coverage of that neighborhood by the inflated graph; its proof was not audited.
qualification_limits: A learned stochastic data augmentation/reduction law, not an exact joint completion/decoder Bayesian posterior.
Its native mean-weight inference is a comparator, not evidence that sampled inference improves quality.
No factorized decoder ensemble or persistent pairing of independent completion/head members is specified in the read method.
The 2026 journal DOI record and 2024 arXiv preprint are title/author-matched metadata; journal method changes were not inspected.
conclusion.adoption: Add a scoped learned-completion/link-decoding prior. Use expected-weight inference as a competent scope-specific comparator only if future work is authorized.
